value.overview: The Veraguan Mango (Anthracothorax veraguensis) is a large, long-tailed hummingbird of southern Central America. It is closely related to the Green-breasted Mango and was formerly treated as part of that species by some authorities. The bird is named for Veraguas in Panama, within much of its known range. It uses forest edges, clearings, gardens, and other habitats with abundant flowering plants, and is an important pollinator of tropical flowers.
value.classification: The Veraguan Mango belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the genus Anthracothorax. It is a member of the mango group of large hummingbirds.
value.identification: This is a large hummingbird with a long, slightly curved bill and a conspicuously long, forked tail. Adults are mainly green, with darker wings and tail feathers. The male has a dark central stripe on the underparts and contrasting blue to purplish coloration on the throat and breast, although appearance can vary with light and viewing angle. Females and immature birds are duller below and may show pale or grayish underparts. Care is needed to distinguish it from the similar Green-breasted Mango.
value.rangeHabitat: The Veraguan Mango occurs in southern Central America, especially Costa Rica and western Panama, with its distribution centered on lowland and foothill areas. In Costa Rica, it is associated mainly with the Pacific side and adjoining southwestern regions, where it may occur in forest edges, secondary growth, plantations, gardens, mangroves, and other partly open habitats. It generally favors places with flowering trees, shrubs, and hummingbird-pollinated plants, and can use human-modified landscapes when suitable nectar sources remain available.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally considered resident or locally dispersive rather than a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, individuals may move short distances in response to flowering conditions, but regular seasonal migration is not well established.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited compared with that of more widespread hummingbirds. Like other Anthracothorax species, the Veraguan Mango is expected to build a small cup-shaped nest, usually in vegetation above the ground, with the female handling incubation and most care of the young. Nest placement may be near forest margins or other open, flower-rich habitats. Timing can vary geographically and may be influenced by rainfall and local flowering cycles.
value.dietFeeding: The Veraguan Mango feeds mainly on nectar from tubular or otherwise hummingbird-pollinated flowers. It also takes small insects and other arthropods, which provide protein, especially during breeding. Its large size and strong flight allow it to defend productive flowers from smaller hummingbirds and other nectar feeders. It may visit flowering trees, shrubs, vines, gardens, and cultivated plants, and can sometimes forage in disturbed habitats with reliable floral resources.
value.behavior: This hummingbird is active and maneuverable, typically hovering while taking nectar and making rapid flights between flowering plants. It may perch conspicuously on exposed twigs while watching its feeding area. Individuals can be territorial around especially rich flowers and may chase other hummingbirds or nectar-feeding birds. Courtship and territorial displays are likely to include aerial pursuits and changes in body posture that emphasize the male’s colorful throat and breast.

conservation.populationTrend: The population trend is not well documented in detail. There is no reliable evidence presented here of a major global decline.
